He was God's own Word, come to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: 'Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts.' He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right.

And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God.' Not that we become gods - but that his own life is opened to us and shared. The point was never only to know about him. The point was to be joined to him - to share in the divine life through the one who entered human nature to heal it from within.

If you want it in one line: the maker, come inside his making, to heal it. And the healing was not information. It was transformation - the whole person turned back toward God, remade from the soul outward. That was why we read Scripture the way we did, why we studied, why we prayed: because every act of learning and worship was meant to bring a soul closer to the Logos himself.

The scriptures - the writings we called Scripture - were our direct connection, and we traced their path as clearly as we could.

We read the four Gospels, the apostolic letters, and the writings of Israel that Jesus himself had read. Origen called the Gospels 'the firstfruits of all Scripture' - the place where the Logos speaks most plainly. We read them aloud in the assembly, week after week, to everyone who came. The literate studied them with teachers. The book and the voice both mattered.

The path we could show runs like this. The apostles wrote or spoke. Their immediate students - the generation after them - received what they wrote and taught what they heard. That deposit was handed down, in writing and in the teaching that traveled with it. By the time our own teachers appear - Clement, then Origen - the scriptures are already fixed in practice and read everywhere, and the rule of faith that guides their reading is named outright as the apostles' own summary, 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles and remaining in the Churches to the present day'.

What we cannot show you - and we will not invent it - is documentary proof for every step of that path between the apostles and our first witnesses. The gap is real. Our confidence rested on three things: unbroken practice as far back as our memory reached, agreement with the other churches we were in communion with, and the match between our rule of faith and the writings themselves.

One more thing. By our last years, the question of which books counted as Scripture had been thought through carefully. Athanasius listed them - 'appointed by the Fathers to be read' - in a letter that survives. But earlier, the edges were less defined. The center was always clear: the four Gospels, Paul, the Torah, the Prophets. The boundary around them took time to settle.

Then you have already done a hard and honest thing by saying it out loud. Among us, not-yet-believing was not failure - it was where nearly everyone began. Our teachers said faith - pistis - is a foundation, not a finish line: something to stand on while the rest is still dark. And we did not ask anyone to force belief. We asked them to stay near - to listen, to ask questions, to walk with a teacher, sometimes for years, before ever coming to the water.

One of our students, Gregory, said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under a teacher he had come to love: 'And so, like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. He was not straining to believe. He was being befriended. The knowing we meant was not agreeing with a list of claims - it was the soul's own change, growing toward God.

We cannot make it happen for you either, and we will not pretend we can. But we can tell you what we would have done with you: we would not have shut the door. We would have said - stay. Ask. Take the time it takes. The Logos - God's own Word, through whom all things were made - meets people where they are, not only where they have already arrived.

Jesus is the Logos - God's own Word and reason, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. That is where we stand, and have stood from the beginning. He is not a creature, not something God made. He is God's own self-expression, as inseparable from the Father as light from its source.

We worshiped him as God before we had the words worked out with full precision. Baptism was always into Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - three names, one movement, one God. But the fight over the wording came late, and it came hard. When Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with a word not found in Scripture - homoousios, 'of one substance' - because every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning of its own.

Here is what stayed constant through all the argument. Only God can join us to God. The whole point of the Incarnation was not to send a messenger with news about God, but for God himself to enter what he made, to heal it from within. Athanasius said it plainest: 'He was made man, so that we might be made God'. That sentence only makes sense if the one who came was genuinely God - otherwise we are being joined to something less, and the promise breaks.

The Spirit, too, is God's own - not a creature, not a lesser power. The three are never alone from one another. But the fullest working-out of how to say that - what later came to be called 'the Trinity' in textbook form - lies mostly beyond our years. What we held was the worship, the conviction, and the fought-for word at Nicaea: the Son is of one substance with the Father, not made.

One God, the maker of all things. He is good, and beyond every image and every clever description. And he is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. (Only after Nicaea was that last part said with full clarity.) God is known the way light is known. You do not stare at the sun; you see everything else by it.

What we held most firmly was that he is always teaching. The whole creation is his school. Scripture is his main lesson. And the slow healing of a soul is his patient method. Our teacher Origen said it plainly: 'every threat and pain and punishment that comes from God is never inflicted in order to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good'. His severity is a physician's, not a torturer's.

We confessed him as maker, but also as healer - entering what he made to repair it from within. The Word through whom all things were made is the same Word who speaks through Scripture, who became flesh in Jesus, who draws a soul toward himself through years of learning. That is why we could say that knowing him changes the knower. He does not stay distant while we study about him. Real knowing is real sharing in his own life.

And he does not force. The soul has real power to turn toward or away. Without that, formation would be manipulation, not growth. He teaches through invitation, through the beauty of truth, through the patient witness of a teacher - not through crushing the will.

When we disagreed about what must be believed, three ways of settling it show in our record - and they sit uneasily beside each other.

Early on, the teachers settled it by argument. They wrote, they lectured, they corresponded. Authority went to visible wisdom - Clement and Origen's authority was earned, not appointed. The student Gregory's own account shows how that worked: a teacher persuaded by the depth and patience of his teaching, not by office.

In the middle years, the bishop's judgment grew. But our clearest picture of that power used well is still argument, not decree. When whole villages in the Arsinoite district came to believe a teaching about the end that Bishop Dionysius thought was wrong, he did not send out a condemnation. He traveled to them, sat down, and argued it through for three days, in public, testing the teaching against Scripture. Everyone listened. He won them over. That is documented - his own account survives.

At the end came the council. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the contested confession for all. The emperor called it. The decision was backed by force.

As for what held across all three: the rule of faith - the short summary the apostles handed down - set the bounds. Origen says plainly that what is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' is what alone can be trusted, and 'that alone is to be believed as truth which differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolical tradition'. Inside those bounds, speculation was honored. Outside them, the boundary was drawn.

The tension is real. At our best, doctrine was settled by patient public persuasion, loving the person while honoring the truth more. At our end, it was settled by councils the emperor called. Both are in our record.

Yes - and not as a problem to be solved, but as the very ground formation worked on.

Our teacher Clement wrote that the Instructor - the Word himself - 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul' not by forcing them out but 'by urging us on'. The struggling itself was treated as material God could work with, not as disqualification from his work. And our method matched that conviction. We asked people preparing for baptism to walk with us, step by step, over a long time - the katechesis - before ever coming to the water. That long road was not testing whether you already believed hard enough; it was the space where belief could actually grow.

One of our students, Gregory, said it happened to him almost from the side: 'like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. He had come to study under Origen, stayed for years, and somewhere in that staying the thing he could not force came on its own. The teacher-student bond was not preparation for formation - it was formation itself.

And when someone fell away entirely - the lapsed, those who gave in under persecution - our hardest struggle was whether to let them back. The strict party said no. The tradition that won here said yes, through repentance - metanoia, the soul truly turned back toward God. Even a deathbed return could be accepted. We were not always good at this - the fights over it were bitter, and our own record does not hide that. But at our best, we held the door open for struggle, not only for certainty.

We believed something real went wrong at the root of humanity. Adam's fall casts its shadow over every soul. Death and disorder are inherited, and no one reaches God unwounded. Our teachers spoke of inherited death and weakness. They also spoke of a fall that each soul signs onto in its own living. 

But here is what we did not say: guilt at birth. The wound is real, universal, and inherited in its effects. We received infant baptism as custom, and we discussed its reason rather than defining it. What stays constant is the direction - the doctor's imagery outweighs the courtroom's. The soul needs healing, not acquittal. It arrives damaged, not condemned.

Scripture is where the Logos speaks - God's own Word addressing a soul that learns to listen. We do not read the scriptures mainly for facts about what once happened, but to meet the one who is speaking now, through the text, to change us. 

Our teachers taught us to read at more than one level. There is the plain sense - what happened, what was said. And there are deeper senses: what the passage says about Christ, what it says to the soul being formed. A single verse holds more than one reading can carry away, and a lifetime of reading opens more than the last year showed. Our own history shows three ways authority was carried, and they moved across our years.

Early on, authority rested on proven wisdom. Teachers argued in books, lectures, and letters. The one whose reading of Scripture and whose way of life showed the greater depth was heard. No title made you authoritative - your words did, or they did not. The school's authority was persuasion, nothing more.

By the middle years, the bishop's judgment had grown. He governed how the community was formed and what it received. When whole villages of the Arsinoite district came to believe a teaching the bishop judged wrong, Dionysius did not send out a condemnation. He traveled to them, sat down for three days of open argument, and won them by persuasion, not force. He writes, 'In many other respects I approve of Nepos and love him - for his faith, his hard work, and his diligence in the Scriptures' - even while he corrected Nepos's teaching. That is our best picture of authority working well: patient, public, loving the man while honoring the truth more.

At the end came the council. Bishops from everywhere ruled for all, at Nicaea, on what must be believed. The emperor called it. The emperor backed it. And after Nicaea, the bishop of Alexandria became the enforcer of that agreed faith across Egypt. Authority had learned to use exile, and saying no could cost a man his place.

So we lived through all three, in one city's lifetime.

Our record leaves the wounds visible. Our greatest teacher was driven out, not by pagans, but by his own bishop. The church remembered both men rather than erasing either. Under persecution, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the community fought bitterly over them. The strict party demanded they stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius defended doing so. After Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation, and some of what was done with that power our own sources report without pride. At our best, we refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable. At our worst, we did what churches with power do. That, too, is in our record.

So here is the actual practice we can show you. When the young man in the story Clement told had fallen away into banditry after his baptism, the Apostle John himself went after him - into the mountains, at risk, refusing to give him up. The path back was long formation, not a single moment. And when whole villages came to believe a teaching their bishop thought was wrong, he traveled to them and argued it through for three days, out loud, testing it against Scripture, loving the people while honoring truth more. That was the style when it worked.

We cannot say the tradition always held to that. We can say it knew the difference between the two, and left both in the record rather than rewriting one out.

No present-day church continues what we were, exactly as we were. Let us say that plainly first, and then say what we can.

In our own time we called ourselves part of the catholic church - the whole church, spread everywhere, as against the sects. It was a claim about wholeness, not the name of a later denomination. We belonged to one baptism, one bread, the scriptures, the rule of faith, and communion with churches across the whole world.

What happened after us broke that unity. The church that sits now in Alexandria is one heir. The churches that hold to Nicaea's confession are others. But between our close and the present day lie splits we did not live through and cannot map from inside our own years. We speak from before those divisions made today's borders.

Here is what we can say honestly. But the exact shape we had, with our particular teachers and our way of holding inquiry and boundary together, is not preserved whole in any single present body.

We will not name one church yours and declare the others not. That would be a judgment reaching past what we can see from where we stand.

Someone who wanted to join us walked a long road - years, not weeks - and the walking was itself the forming. That is the first thing to say plainly: we did not hand over the faith at the door and call it done. We led people through it, step by step, until they were ready to stand in the water.

It began with wanting. Not with agreeing to a list of claims, but with the soul's first real turn toward God - pistis, we called it, faith as a movement, not a verdict. Someone heard, or saw something in how we lived, and came asking. And we let them stay near - to listen, to watch, sometimes for a long time before any teaching began at all. Gregory, one of our students, said it came to him almost from the side, while he walked with a teacher he had come to love: 'like a spark falling on our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. He was not straining to believe. He was being befriended.

Then came the teaching itself - the katechesis, the long instruction. For some, this meant sitting under a teacher in the school, where learning was not preparation for formation but formation itself: the mind's turning, the soul's questioning, the slow change that came from wrestling with Scripture under a guide who had walked the road ahead. For others - the majority, who could not read or had no access to the school - it meant hearing the Scriptures read aloud in the assembly, year after year, and being taught their meaning by a deacon or the bishop. Either way, the teaching was patient. Clement said plainly that our Instructor - the Word himself - 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul by urging us on,' not by rushing us. The whole point was a real turning of the person toward God, and that takes the time it takes.

The teaching itself had a shape. At its foundation was the rule of faith - the short summary of what the apostles handed down, which set the bounds for everything else. Beyond that, the Scriptures were opened. And here is where our teaching went deepest. We read them not as a record of what God once said, but as the Logos speaking now, through the text, to a soul formed to hear. Origen taught that 'just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does Scripture' - meaning it could be read at more than one level, and the deeper senses opened only to those who had been prepared to receive them. Reading Scripture at depth was not a skill we taught; it was the primary instrument by which we formed people. The reader was transformed by the reading, not merely informed.

At the end of the road came the water. Baptism was not a ceremony announcing a choice already made. It was a real crossing - the body sharing in Christ's death and rising, the light of new birth given in the flesh. And after the water, the table: the bread and the cup, the thanksgiving meal that was ours to share.

Here is what we cannot show you, because the record does not give it: how long each stage lasted, exactly what the teaching covered in what order, how the villages outside the city adapted the pattern. The school's method we can describe from the teachers' own books. The whole-community pattern we can see in its results - everyone baptized, everyone fed - but not in its documented steps. We are telling you what we can show, and naming plainly where the ground thins.

The first thing we did with an unsettled mind was receive it, not fix it. Our teaching was patient - years patient, sometimes. One of the travelers who came to us late in our time met an old teacher, blind from boyhood, who had spent sixty years in the school: Didymus, the master who never saw a written page but knew Scripture through. The traveler does not say the man offered quick comfort. He says he stayed and learned. That patience was our first answer.

The second thing was the practice itself - not as a cure, but as a path to walk while the mind was still working. We had the water, the table, the set times of prayer. Those were not conditional on your certainty. They were the frame that held you while doubt did its work. Clement said the Instructor - the Word himself - 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul by urging us on,' not by shutting the questions down. And our whole method rested on the conviction that God himself is always teaching - through Scripture's difficulty, through the catechesis, even through what troubles you. An unsettled mind, to us, was not a verdict of failure. It was the condition under which real formation could happen.

What we did not have was a formula for making it stop. We had a community that stayed with you, teachers whose authority rested on visible wisdom rather than a title, and the daily rhythm of bread and prayer. And we had the conviction that repentance - metanoia - is not feeling sorry but the soul truly turning back to God, and that turning takes the time it takes.

Yes - but not as a slogan, and never as a one-time emotional moment standing alone.

Our teachers used the image of new birth plainly. To be baptized was called being enlightened - photismos - the light of new sight given. And it was a real crossing, in the body, into Christ's death and rising - not a ceremony marking a choice already made, but the threshold itself. 

But here is what that crossing looked like among us. It came at the end of a long road. People preparing for baptism - the catechumens - walked that road for years, not weeks: learning Scripture, unlearning old habits, being formed by a teacher and by the community's life together. The water was the moment the whole thing turned visible and irrevocable, not the moment formation began.

And after the water, the road kept going. Our whole understanding of the person was that you are made for God - the image of God is in you from the beginning, and formation is that image growing into likeness. Being baptized did not end that growth. It opened it.

So yes, we spoke of new birth. But never as though the soul's turning happened in one afternoon, and never as though saying the words once settled everything. The turning was real. The road was long. And the community walked it with you, before and after.

The life you are asking me to describe — I cannot give it to you as one person's day, because the distance between lives was real. The learned man who studied at the school lived a different day than the dockworker's household. The consecrated widow's rhythm was not the same as the mother with six children. And our record comes almost entirely from the school side of that line — so what I can show you is uneven, and I will name the unevenness as I go.

For someone in the school's reach — a student, or a household with the means and learning for it — the day turned on Scripture. It was read, discussed, prayed. Formation was not a task added to the day; it was woven into how the hours moved. The Instructor — that was one of our names for the Logos — was at work through all of it: 'Our Instructor, the Word, cures the unnatural desires of the soul, and he does this by urging us on'. Study was not preparation for devotion; it was devotion. The teacher's voice, the opened text, the question asked and corrected — that was the soul turning Godward, step by step.

For the majority — those who could not read, or whose labor filled the day — we cannot show you the same detail, because they left almost no writing. But we can show you where their day touched ours. The assembly gathered. Scripture was read aloud. Baptism asked nothing of your letters. And in crisis, the household was where it lived or died. When plague emptied the streets, it was not the learned who nursed the sick and buried the dead — or not only them. Dionysius wrote it plainly: 'Most of our people held nothing back in their overflowing love and kindness toward one another'. The day's ordinary work became the soul's training ground when the crisis came.

The household itself — the oikos — held more than our writings often show. It was where children learned the faith, where the enslaved and the free lived under one roof, and where mothers carried weight our record barely names. We have one story of a mother hiding her young son's clothes to keep him from running to his own death. The record does not even give her a name. That tells you where the weight was, and also what got written down.

So here is the honest answer. If you were among the few the school could reach, your day was Scripture, prayer, a teacher's voice, and the slow work of a soul being reordered toward God. If you were not, your day was labor, the assembly when it gathered, and the household where faith actually passed. Both are real. One left us almost all the pages. The life you are asking for is in both, but I can only show you the one our record chose to save.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. Our own writings describe souls and books far more than rooms and walls. The city itself has kept little: it was rebuilt age after age, and much of the old shore now lies under the sea.

What we can say is what we gathered around. The table for the eucharistia - the thanksgiving, the bread and cup. A chair for the teacher. A place for the scriptures to be read aloud. The assembly itself - the ekklesia - was not the building but the people gathered around the Logos who called them. One of our teachers mentioned silver couches, little dishes for vinegar, platters and bowls in wealthy homes, when he was teaching about how believers should live. That tells you something about where some of us met - in houses, not always purpose-built halls.

But here is what we must say plainly: the school tradition that shaped so much of our thought may not have left a formal building to find. What is well attested is the teachers and the students; whether it was an institution with walls and a registry is disputed. The weight of our record fell on what changed in the soul, not on what you could measure with a surveyor's line. That is an honest limit, not an evasion.

They gave up their old gods - that much is certain. The teaching-time before baptism - we called it katechesis - could last years, and during it a person learned to see their whole life differently: who they prayed to, how they spent their money, what they did with their bodies. When they finally came to the water - we called it photismos, illumination - they were crossing a real line. The old sacrifices stopped. The old festival days no longer bound them. Their household gods went quiet.

Beyond that, what it cost depended on who you were and when you came. For some it meant leaving professions - there were trades we would not baptize people into, though our sources do not give us the full list. For the wealthy, Clement taught that possessions themselves were not the problem - 'gold, silver, houses, as gifts from God' - but the grip had to loosen. Formation was about the soul's direction, not the purse's emptying. For others, in the years of danger, it could cost them everything. The father of one of our greatest teachers was beheaded for his faith. That teacher himself nearly ran out to join him - only his mother's quick thinking stopped him.

But here is what we cannot show you, because our record does not hold it: what the ordinary member, in the villages, in the years of peace, actually gave up day by day. The city teachers wrote about wealth and idols. The country churches appear in our ink mostly once, when their bishop spent three days persuading them about Scripture. What they gave up in the ordinary grain of their weeks - that we do not have in their own words.

Marriage was real among us, and honored - not despised as some taught, but held as good, a place where souls are formed. Clement wrote a whole book defending it against those who said the body was shame and married life beneath the spiritual. That book survives in the Greek he wrote it in, but we have no English rendering we can honestly offer you. So we can give you the heart, not the fine grain.

The heart was this: marriage was lasting, honorable, a school for virtue in the household - the oikos, where most people were actually formed. Children learned the faith there, the household prayed there, and the married state was not set against holiness. We also honored consecrated celibacy - the virgins and widows who stood apart - but we did not make marriage the lesser road.

How it was marked - the ceremony, the witnesses, what vows were spoken - our sources leave mostly quiet. What stands clear is that it was public, it bound, and the community recognized it as binding. Whether there was a blessing in the assembly, whether a presbyter presided, how it connected to baptism and the Eucharist: these are things our surviving writings do not spell out for us, and we will not invent them.

What we can say plainly: marriage was not a private contract. It belonged to the household and the community both. And the finer detail we must leave in the sources rather than guess at.

Yes. The two ways we had of being serious about God - they sat together uneasily, and we felt it.

One way was to die for Christ. When the persecutions came, some believers stood before the magistrate and would not sacrifice, and paid for it with their lives. Potamiaena was one. And the contemplative path took years, letters, a teacher. Most believers had none of those. So which was the real shape of Christian seriousness - the one open to all through blood, or the one open to the few through books?

I am a representative of Alexandrian Christianity, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what we can tell you honestly.

Not through the school first. That door belonged mostly to those who could read and argue in Greek - we will tell you that plainly, not smooth it over. The school reached the few, and if you had been among them, you would have found a teacher who worked with questions, not around them. Gregory, one of our students, said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under a teacher he had come to love: 'like some spark lighting upon our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. That path was real, but it was not the only path, and it was not most people's path.

But the school was never the whole of us. What reached everyone was the water and the table: baptism asked nothing of your letters, and the same bread, the same cup, was set before whoever had walked the road to it. That door, at least, we can show you was open. The catechesis - the teaching that led to baptism - took time, sometimes years, and it worked with doubt rather than demanding its absence first. Our teachers said faith is a foundation, not a finish line. You could ask. You could take the time it took.

And there was the household - the oikos - where most people were actually formed. Not a private family, but the whole household, where children learned the prayers and the stories and the way of living from the people who raised them. If you had been part of a believing household, that is where formation would have happened for you, more than in any lecture room.

What we held about how life should be lived, we held firmly, and some of it will feel hard to you. When you ask about any particular thing, we will tell you what we held, plainly, without softening it. But the holding was never the door. The door was Christ, and baptism was the crossing. On the other side of it, you would have found the bread, the assembly, and a community that believed every person bore the image of God and could be changed by knowing him.

What is it about yourself you are asking us to see?

We were not handed a settled map of anyone's fate, and we will not draw one. Here is what we held. Judgment is real: what we do matters, and God is not mocked. Something went wrong at the root of humanity, and its shadow falls over every soul. But our teachers said something about God's severity that set us apart. Origen wrote that every threat and pain and punishment that comes from God is never inflicted to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good. Punishment, in our teaching, was a physician's fire, not a torturer's.

Some among us - Origen most boldly - hoped further still: the apokatastasis, the restoration of all things, that God's healing might in the end reach every creature. We must be careful with you there. That was a teacher's hope, and a contested one, never our settled doctrine. It was the kind of question Origen treated as open ground - what Scripture does not settle plainly, a soul may explore as part of its own formation.

As for those outside our community: Clement taught that God had been at work among the Greeks all along - that even their philosophy had been given as a schoolmaster to lead them toward Christ. We did not think God's reach ended at our door. Whether any particular person stands within his mercy is not ours to rule. That he is the kind of God whose fire heals - that, we did hold.
